speaker: Jordan Teague
text: Yeah. And it seems to me like "AI native" is typically just a signal for "we bought a ChatGPT subscription and added our associates to it." speaker: George Campbell
text: No, but this is a whole separate podcast episode. My dad was general counsel of a publicly traded company. We've represented a lot of large companies. speaker: Jordan Teague
text: And why do you predict that day is coming?

speaker: George Campbell
text: Well, first of all, it's never been a good excuse. And I think there was enough cover, and there's obviously corporate culture that wants to cover entrenched management. Again, this is a whole separate podcast, but with the advent of AI and the ability... I often like to think of it as, it's really like a prosthesis for knowledge work. In many ways, we think of automobiles as separate machines, but they've evolved into being a human prosthesis for mobility. AI is a tool. It amplifies and allows smaller groups of people to do more with less. So I think you're going to see... I had a conversation this week with a plaintiff's firm, and he's using another platform on the plaintiff's side that has been gaining some popularity now with venture funding. And it's allowing him, as a solo with two paralegals, to do stuff that heretofore was impossible. And I think Big Law, and the whole idea of "we're just going to throw as much paper and people as possible" as a defense tactic, is not as effective anymore. So for many of those reasons, like I said, I think it could be a whole separate podcast, but this whole idea of "I just hired the biggest, most expensive firm I could find" is going away. That makes absolutely no sense. It's like, firm or no firm, results matter. People want to pay for results. speaker: Jordan Teague
text: Well, yeah, everyone loves a little good old-fashioned prestige maxing every now and then.

speaker: Jordan Teague

speaker: George Campbell
text: Yeah, you asked me that, and I dodged the question. I think real AI adoption... and we even have to define what is AI, or superintelligence. I think the government changed the name again. What is that? We really don't have a clear definition of that. But I think if you look at using that prosthesis, and if you were going to ask me my personal opinion, I would say, all right, you've been doing a lot of deep dives into Claude. I've been working with Grok as we've been testing these systems, and working with Copilot as well. I think real AI adoption doesn't happen until you have something like, if you've seen the Iron Man movie, Jarvis, where I've got a Jarvis on in real time with me all the time, voice activated, like you would say "Hey Siri" to your iPhone. You're just talking to it and having it run tasks whenever you think about it. And no typing. There's no one typing anything in, and I can just say, "Hey Jarvis, go research this file," or "Hey Jarvis, listen to this meeting we're about to sit in on, and then go ahead and do all the conflicts check and get an engagement letter set up for the client to sign." That, I think, is real AI enabled. And to use the prosthesis analogy, you're wearing it while you're working. That's truly AI enabled. speaker: Jordan Teague
text: So I feel like another hot debate right now, when it comes to judgment in the legal profession, is the fate of junior lawyers. And what I perceive is a little bit of an assumption that the role of the junior is going to greatly diminish, because it's just faster for a senior lawyer to do it themselves with AI. What say thee of that?

speaker: George Campbell
text: I think that's making a future prediction using present assumptions. And you either have to make a future prediction using future assumptions, or a present prediction using present assumptions. But it's the wrong mental map. Depending on who you read or who you believe, lawyers right now, or access to legal services, is limited to only about maybe 20%, in some cases 30, at most 40% of the population. I don't know any other market where, by the use of technology, your total addressable market could double. And so with those junior lawyers, right now it's not cost-effective for them to handle a $5,000 fender bender or a small contract dispute. You just settle it, walk away, write it off. Well, now those types of disputes are very cost-effective for a junior lawyer to handle. So I think you will still see a lot of junior lawyers working, perhaps on smaller-stakes matters, because they can do it cheaper and the stakes are lower, so the client is not as upset if you screw it up. And at the end of the day, it's kind of like the problem we had in crypto with on-ramp and off-ramp. There's got to be a human review off-ramp for this stuff. You can't just plug it into the machine and go full send and let the automation go. At least until we replace the court system and human nature. But there's got to be human review, and I think you're just going to see more work that more juniors have got to spend time reviewing. And if it's lower-stakes stuff, well, then they'll be content with a junior review, and only the higher-stakes things should go to the senior review. But the dirty little secret is every other business in the world runs like that. There's no reason law firms shouldn't as well. And if they are, the only reason they're doing that is to run up the bill so they can get their billable hours in.

speaker: Jordan Teague
text: Right. Yeah, I think you make a really good point that making future predictions with present facts is typically ill-advised. I think also the loudest people in the room right now about AI are probably the ones who tend to have a hard time finding ROI with delegation in the first place. And, you know, I'll even throw myself under the bus with that too. We all know that my favorite thing to do is just lock myself in a room for 12 hours with a laptop and see what kind of magic comes out of there. So I get it. I really do. But it's me and everyone like me who's screaming on Twitter and on LinkedIn about this. It has never been faster in the short term to delegate and train, for anyone. Never. The ROI on delegation requires an investment, and that investment has always been time. And so the question is not, "Is it faster in the short term for me to do it myself with AI?" Because obviously the answer is yes. The question is: does AI change the ROI equation? Does it make the ROI greater? Does it keep it the same? Does it diminish it? Does it eliminate it? A lot of people think it's going to eliminate it, but let's be honest, you're making that prediction based on vibes. And that's fine. You're entitled to do that. But I don't think that we should throw decades of wisdom on the management of a professional services firm out the window just because we have this new technology.

speaker: George Campbell
text: Yeah. I mean, a good previous example would be runners. Back in the day, which I caught the tail end of when I started my career, before electronic filing... and luckily my office was in the courthouse, so I didn't have to go that far to file something.

speaker: Jordan Teague
text: What's a runner, for people who don't know?

speaker: George Campbell
text: So you had to go physically to the courthouse to file something, or send it by registered mail with multiple copies for the clerk to stamp: one for them, one for the opposing party and one for you. Wait for that to come back, and then serve it on the other side. And then once you've got proof of service, mail that back to the clerk. Well, if you wanted to do anything without waiting two or three weeks for all that mail to go back and forth, you had runners, and they were just couriers for law firms who would run down to the clerk, run it back to your office, run it over to opposing counsel, give it to the process server to take and go serve it on everybody. So you had a courier who could do that. And then this magical technology called email came along. And that did eliminate the runner as a job description, and it was an entry-level point for a law firm. But lawyers have not stopped hiring entry-level people. They're now doing different things like intake, or managing the docket, or calendaring, or secretary work, whatever, reviewing discovery. So that didn't go away. The job just shifted. There's still just as many people working in law firms as there were 30 years ago when runners were a profession. It's just humans are doing a different task, because the computer handles the filing.

speaker: Jordan Teague
text: Okay. Well, I'm running tight on time, because I need to go argue with Claude about something that it's doing wrong that I could have done faster myself. But before we close, what is one spicy prediction that you have on where this is all headed in our profession?

speaker: George Campbell
text: That's a great question. And I hate it when people say "that's a great question," because it's just a filler to say, "I don't know the answer and I'm trying to buy time to think about it." So I'm working on not saying that. One spicy prediction I have is that in the short term, we are going to see an explosion in legal demand, particularly as a byproduct of what we call the slopocalypse, because lawyers, especially unscrupulous lawyers, no matter what the consequences have always been, they're going to keep sending in slop and trying not to get caught. But even worse, pro se litigants are going to mob the court system, because now there's this power-to-the-people element. And a good example of what was the very frontier of this was DoNotPay.com. But now you can have your Claude bot go track down the spam caller who's been wearing you out, get all their information, and then launch a TCPA complaint. So I think the court systems are not ready for this slopocalypse. They have their head in the sand, and the judges need to take note and get ahead of this problem. Simple fixes could be page limits on briefs, or asking for leave of the court to do more filing, raising the cost of filing fees, which absolutely needs to happen. It makes no sense that a $20 million lawsuit and a $500 lawsuit have the same filing fee. That doesn't mean you should go crazy and be punitive, but they are not equipped. They do not have the staff or the resources to handle a flood of pro se litigation, which I think in the short term is going to happen, and they need to get out ahead of it.
